issues.legal_issue: The freedom to acquire, own, and dispose of property does not protect concrete rights in particular property.
material_facts: The challenge concerned a purchaser’s specific rights in an estate, including the right to annul certain under-tenures and evict under-tenants.
The purchaser argued that legislation retrospectively curtailing those rights violated the constitutional freedom relating to property.
issues.conclusion: The concrete property rights at issue were not protected by the freedom to acquire, own, and dispose of property; their protection was governed by the constitutional provisions specifically addressing property.
issues.legal_principle: Article 19(1)(f) protects a citizen’s general capacity to acquire, own, and dispose of property, not the concrete rights attached to particular property; concrete property rights are addressed by Article 31. The Chief Justice relied on the distinction between fundamental capacities and rights in specific property discussed in Butchers Union etc. Co. v. Crescent City etc. Co. and rejected applying the approach to Article 19(1)(f) that had been considered in A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras.

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A person challenges the constitutional validity of a law.
predicates.claim_concerns_specific_property_rights: The claim concerns rights attached to particular property rather than a general capacity to own property.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns rights attached to particular property, those rights are not protected by the general freedom to own property.

issues.legal_issue: A law that curtails an incident of property ownership does not deprive the owner of property unless the curtailment substantially withholds possession or enjoyment, seriously impairs use and enjoyment, or materially reduces value.
material_facts: A purchaser acquired an estate at a revenue sale with a right to annul certain under-tenures and evict certain under-tenants.
A later law applied retrospectively to pending proceedings and curtailed that right.
The purchaser retained the estate and could continue to enjoy it in other respects.
The amended law gave the purchaser an expanded ability to seek increased rent from tenure holders and tenants brought within the protection of the law.
issues.conclusion: The retrospective curtailment was not a deprivation of property under Article 31(1) or Article 31(2); the constitutional challenge failed, and the law did not require compensation on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 31(1) and 31(2) are not mutually exclusive: they address the protection of property from State deprivation, and the deprivation contemplated in clause (1) corresponds to acquisition or taking possession under clause (2). Whether a curtailment amounts to deprivation depends on its effect in the particular case; it is substantial if it withholds property from the owner’s possession and enjoyment, seriously impairs its use and enjoyment, or materially reduces its value. The Chief Justice relied on A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras, P.D. Shamdasani v. Central Bank of India, and Minister of State for the Army v. Dalziel, and distinguished the contrary approach expressed by Das J. in Chiranjit Lal Chaudhury v. Union of India.

rule.if: property_deprivation_challenge and law_retroactively_curtailed_an_ownership_right and owner_retained_the_property_and_general_enjoyment and other_ownership_rights_remained and law_granted_a_countervailing_rent_right

predicates.property_deprivation_challenge: A person challenges a law on the ground that it deprived them of property.
predicates.law_retroactively_curtailed_an_ownership: A law applied retrospectively and curtailed a right attached to property.
predicates.owner_retained_the_property_and_general_: The owner retained the property and could continue to enjoy it in other respects.
predicates.other_ownership_rights_remained: The owner retained other incidents of ownership over the property.
predicates.law_granted_a_countervailing_rent_right: The law gave the owner an expanded right to seek rent from persons whose interests it protected.

issues.definition: When a retrospective law curtails an ownership right but the owner retains the property and its general enjoyment, keeps other ownership rights, and receives a countervailing rent right, the curtailment does not amount to constitutional deprivation of property.
